episodes.title: Why are airplane windows round?
episodes.summary: Square windows would show more sky. So why does every airplane have round ones?

episodes.title: Why do airplane windows have a tiny hole?
episodes.summary: Look closely at an airplane window and you'll find a tiny hole. Fitz wants to plug it. Should he?

episodes.title: Why are stop signs octagons?
episodes.summary: Fitz wants a round stop sign. Gauge wants to know: is round already taken?

episodes.title: Why do pen caps have a hole in the top?
episodes.summary: Gauge wants to seal that “pointless” hole for fresher ink. Fitz says not so fast.

episodes.title: Why do train tracks sit on rocks?
episodes.summary: Piles of rocks look messy. Gauge wants to lay the tracks on plain dirt. Will dirt hold?

episodes.title: Why do bridges have bumpy metal gaps?
episodes.summary: Those ka-thunk gaps are annoying, so Gauge wants to fill them in. What are they for?

episodes.title: How do woodpeckers not hurt their brains?
episodes.summary: Woodpeckers bang their heads into trees thousands of times a day. How is their brain okay?

episodes.title: Why do brick walls have little holes at the bottom?
episodes.summary: Those little gaps at the bottom of brick walls look like a mistake. Gauge wants to seal them. Should he?

episodes.title: How do bees build hexagons?
episodes.summary: Bees build their honeycomb out of hexagons. Gauge thinks circles would be better. Why six sides?

episodes.title: Why don't birds get shocked on power lines?
episodes.summary: Birds sit on live wires all day. Gauge wants to give them rubber boots. Do they need them?

episodes.title: Why do the F and J keys have bumps?
episodes.summary: Two keys on every keyboard have tiny bumps. Gauge wants to sand them off. What are they for?

episodes.title: Why do some skyscrapers have a giant ball inside?
episodes.summary: Some towers hang a giant ball near the top. Gauge wants to cut it out. Why is it there?

episodes.title: Why are manhole covers round?
episodes.summary: Gauge wants a square manhole cover to match the paving. Is round just tradition?

episodes.title: Why do jet engines have a spiral in the middle?
episodes.summary: Many jet engines have a white spiral in the middle. Gauge wants to paint it plain. What's it for?

episodes.title: Why was this NYC skyscraper secretly repaired at night?
episodes.summary: Case Files: a 59-story tower on stilts, a hidden weakness, and welders working through the night. Gauge has red string. Lots of it.

episodes.title: Why did the Golden Gate Bridge start humming?
episodes.summary: Case Files: in 2020, people across San Francisco heard the bridge hum. The answer runs through a bridge experts said couldn't be built, its orange paint, and a bridge built to move.

episodes.title: Why do sidewalks have lines?
episodes.summary: Sidewalks are covered in straight grooves. Gauge wants to smooth them over. Why are they there?

episodes.title: How do cats land on their feet?
episodes.summary: A falling cat flips right side up in midair. Gauge thinks it pushed off something. Did it?

episodes.title: Why do some plugs have a third round prong?
episodes.summary: Some plugs have a round third prong. Gauge wants to snip it off. What does it do?

episodes.title: Why do bathroom sinks have a little hole near the top?
episodes.summary: There's a little hole near the top of most bathroom sinks. Gauge wants to plug it. What's it for?

episodes.title: Why do tall buildings have revolving doors?
episodes.summary: Revolving doors are slow. Gauge wants a normal door instead. Why do tall buildings use them?

episodes.title: Why do airplane wings curve up at the tips?
episodes.summary: Many airplane wings bend up at the tips. Gauge wants to straighten them. What do they do?

episodes.title: Why do some roads have grooves cut into them?
episodes.summary: Some roads have grooves cut into them. Gauge wants to pave them smooth. Should he?

episodes.title: Why did Chicago lift its streets and buildings?
episodes.summary: Case Files: Chicago set out to lift a whole hotel, turned its river around, and dug a giant tunnel. Gauge keeps score in the city's long fight with its own water.

episodes.title: Why are fire hydrants painted different colors?
episodes.summary: Hydrant caps come in different colors. Gauge wants them all the same. Are the colors a code?

episodes.title: How do geckos stick to walls?
episodes.summary: Geckos walk up glass. Gauge is sure they use suction cups. Do they?

episodes.title: Why do most wind turbines have three blades?
episodes.summary: Most wind turbines have three blades. Gauge wants to add more. Would that help?

episodes.title: Why is there a little arrow by your fuel gauge?
episodes.summary: There's a tiny arrow next to the fuel gauge. Gauge wants to scrape it off. What does it point to?

episodes.title: Why do ceiling tiles have tiny holes?
episodes.summary: Office ceiling tiles are full of tiny holes. Gauge wants to fill them in. What are they for?

episodes.title: Why do big ships have a round bump under the front?
episodes.summary: Big ships have a round bump under the waterline at the front. Gauge wants to cut it off. Why is it there?

episodes.title: Why do some roads have little raised reflectors on the lines?
episodes.summary: Some road lines have little raised bumps on them. Gauge wants to scrape them off. What are they for?
